explicit_definitions_given: Testimony as a performative speech act
Quasi-judicial trial as structural site of truth-disclosure
Holy Ghost as divine epistemic tribunal

objections_raised: Confessional pole risks solipsism (private feeling without objective truth)
Narratival pole risks dead orthodoxy (mere recitation of facts without living faith)
How can a timeless subjective assurance verify a temporal objective fact?

method_and_evidence.evidence_type: Conceptual analysis, scriptural exegesis, philosophical synthesis

philosophical_orientation.grounding: Continental philosophy (Ricoeurian hermeneutics) synthesized with analytic philosophy of language (speech act theory)
philosophical_orientation.thematic_focus: Epistemology of religious belief, philosophy of testimony, philosophical theology, philosophy of law

structural_organization.structure_type: Partitioned essay with progressive deepening (Ricoeur -> LDS theology -> Abinadi narrative -> Eschatological synthesis)

summary_of_core_decisions: The text resolves the subjective/objective paradox of testimony by redefining it as a performative speech act that operates within a dual-jurisdictional (human/divine) quasi-judicial structure. The Holy Ghost provides the epistemic guarantee (subjective), while the historical narrative provides the ontic anchor (objective). The willingness to suffer (martyrdom) serves as the somatic proof that unifies the poles, inverting the human verdict into a divine one and transforming testimony into an active eschatological intervention.

thesis_commitment.hedging_density_in_final_paragraph: Low - the conclusion is assertive and definitive regarding the performative nature of testimony
